## Welcome {#home}

### International Health

**Learning Objectives:**

- Trace the organizations that preceded WHO and what it inherited from them
- Describe WHO's governance structure and India's regional office
- State the purpose and core capacities required under the International Health Regulations (2005)
- Identify the roles of UNICEF, the World Bank, the Global Fund, and Gavi in global health
- Name further UN and bilateral/philanthropic contributors to international health
- Define global health security and health diplomacy

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This chapter closes the Global Perspectives section and the full

## Evolution of International Health Organizations {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

WHO did not emerge in isolation — it consolidated a century of earlier,
fragmented efforts:

`International Sanitary Conferences (from 1851, Paris — quarantine coordination, no lasting agreement) → Pan American Sanitary Bureau (1902, the world's first international health agency) → Office International d'Hygiène Publique (1907, Paris — communicable disease intelligence) → Health Organization of the League of Nations (1923) → UNRRA (1943) → WHO (1948)`

**Why this history matters:** each predecessor contributed something WHO
still uses — the Pan American Sanitary Bureau became **PAHO**, WHO's
regional office for the Americas; the League's Health Organization
pioneered the **expert-committee model** and periodic epidemiological
reporting that WHO still runs today.

---

## WHO Governance, Revisited {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Building on Chapter 1's brief introduction:

- **World Health Assembly** — WHO's supreme decision-making body,
  composed of all member states, sets policy and elects the
  Director-General
- **Six regional offices** — India falls under **WHO-SEARO** (South-East
  Asia Regional Office)
- WHO's core functions extend beyond technical guidance: it also serves
  as the custodian of the binding international legal instrument covered
  next — the International Health Regulations

---

## International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

The IHR (2005) is a **legally binding international instrument**,
covering all 194 WHO member states (196 States Parties in total).

**Purpose:** to prevent, protect against, control, and provide a public
health response to the **international spread of disease**, in ways
proportionate to public health risk — while avoiding unnecessary
interference with international traffic and trade.

**Core capacities countries must maintain:**

- Early warning and routine **surveillance** systems
- **Epidemiological and outbreak investigation** skills
- **Laboratory** expertise
- Information and communication technology systems
- Management systems, including a designated **National IHR Focal
  Point** for communicating with WHO

**Direct link to Chapter 6:** IHR is the legal framework requiring every
country to be capable of the outbreak-investigation steps already
covered there.

---

## Global Health Financing and Delivery Actors {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Beyond WHO, several other organizations shape global health outcomes:

- **UNICEF** — child-focused UN agency; procures the large majority of
  vaccine commodities used in global immunization programmes
- **World Bank** — a major financer of health systems globally, shaping
  health policy through lending and technical influence
- **The Global Fund** (to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria) —
  responds to high-impact communicable diseases in resource-poor
  countries, including broader health-systems support
- **Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance** — a public-private partnership (WHO,
  UNICEF, World Bank, vaccine industry, donor governments, civil
  society) that has helped immunize **over 1.2 billion children**,
  preventing more than 20.6 million deaths, and helped **halve child
  mortality** in 78 lower-income countries since 2000

---

## Other UN and Partner Agencies {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Beyond WHO/UNICEF/World Bank/Gavi, several further UN specialized
agencies and external partners have shaped health outcomes in India and
globally:

| Agency | Focus |
|---|---|
| **UNDP** (1966) | Broad development financing/technical assistance across sectors, health included |
| **UNFPA** | Population and reproductive health programming; assisting India since 1974 |
| **FAO** (1945) | Food production and nutrition; ran the World Freedom from Hunger Campaign (1960) |
| **ILO** (1919) | Labour/occupational health standards — the *International Labour Code* |

**Bilateral and philanthropic contributors** have also mattered
historically: USAID (malaria eradication, family planning support), the
**Colombo Plan** (helped establish AIIMS New Delhi), and the
**Rockefeller** and **Ford Foundations** (medical education, rural
health service pilots, and institutions including AIIMS and the
National Institute of Virology, Pune).

---

## Global Health Security {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Global health security** refers to defence against internal and
external public health risks and threats — spanning protection against
cross-border infectious disease spread **and** ensuring access to
essential medicines and health services. The concept was formally linked
to epidemic alert and response by a **2001 World Health Assembly
resolution**.

**Connects directly to Chapter 6's herd immunity and outbreak-control
concepts** — but scaled to the level of international cooperation rather
than a single country's response.

---

## Health Diplomacy {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Health diplomacy** sits at the interface between international health
assistance and international political relations — using negotiation,
advocacy, and cross-sector collaboration (health and foreign affairs
together) to advance global health goals. It's a relatively young and
still-evolving field within international relations theory, reflecting
how health crises increasingly require coordinated action across
national borders and sectors that traditionally operated separately.

---

## Gavi's Public-Private Partnership Model {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Gavi's structure — bringing together governments, WHO, UNICEF, the World
Bank, vaccine manufacturers, and philanthropic funders (e.g. the Gates
Foundation) under one financing and delivery mechanism — is often cited
as a model for how global health initiatives can pool diverse
stakeholders' comparative advantages, beyond what any single
international organization could achieve alone. Gavi also funds global
vaccine stockpiles for diseases like Ebola, cholera, meningococcal
disease, and yellow fever.

---

## From National Program to International Architecture {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

This chapter completes a thread running through much of this curriculum:
national programmes like Universal Immunization (Chapter 14), Ayushman
Bharat (Chapter 11), and NSCAEM (Chapter 15) don't operate in isolation —
they exist within, and are often financially or technically supported
by, this wider international architecture of WHO governance, binding
regulation (IHR), and global financing partnerships (Gavi, Global Fund,
World Bank).
